units.title: A paper door and a hat in the wind
units.alignmentNote: Two complete written four-question passages for junior2 explicitly adapt the written-reading part of its source. Junior3 retains a four-email thread with five questions plus a separate five-question reading, all three-choice. No source prose copied.

materials.title: The door in the model house
materials.text:
Our art group made a model house for the school display. I drew windows, painted a roof and cut a small door in the front. The door opened beautifully, but it opened outwards into the path we had drawn for visitors.

At first, I thought that did not matter because nobody could really walk inside a cardboard house. Our teacher asked what the model was intended to communicate. We were not making a real building, but we were showing an idea about how one might work.

We placed paper figures on the path. When the door opened, it pushed one figure away. The drawing had looked spacious from above, yet the moving part occupied space that the flat plan did not make obvious. We changed the doorway position and checked it again.

The roof then became a problem. It hid the rooms from anyone looking through the front. We made it removable, with a label inviting visitors to lift it gently. The model could now show an outside view and an interior arrangement without pretending the two were visible at once.

At the display, some visitors admired the colours, while others asked about the paper figures. I liked both kinds of attention. The model did not prove our design could be built. It allowed us to discuss features that a single drawing had left unclear. I had spent most of my first evening painting, but the useful changes came from imagining what could move and where a person would need to stand.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the first door arrangement?
options: It opens into the visitor path
questions.explanation: Opening door uses path space. It opens/coloured wall present, not roof.

questions.prompt: Why does the teacher ask about the model’s purpose?
options: To replace every model with a painting
To forbid any discussion of buildings
To claim a cardboard house must be lived in
To connect its details with what it should communicate
questions.explanation: Model communicates design use, not actual habitation. Other claims unsupported.

questions.prompt: What do paper figures help reveal?
options: The exact weight of a real roof
The space occupied by the moving door
questions.explanation: Figures show path interference. Other information not measured by placement.

questions.prompt: Why is the roof made removable?
options: To show the interior as well as the outside
questions.explanation: Removal reveals hidden rooms. No engineering guarantee/disappearance/question ban.

materials.title: A hat after the wind
materials.text:
My grandfather lost his hat during a windy walk beside the river. It rolled across the grass and stopped near a fence. I ran after it, proud that I could reach it before he did. When I picked it up, however, I found a small hole in the cloth.

I expected him to be upset. He looked at it, checked the band inside and said he had worn the hat for many years. The hole did not make the whole hat disappear. We could ask someone who repaired clothes whether it could be fixed.

At home, he showed me a photograph from a holiday. The same hat was on his head, although its colour looked brighter then. He remembered the place partly through the clothes people wore. An object could carry a history without needing to remain exactly as it had first appeared.

The repairer added a neat patch. Grandfather chose a colour close to the original but did not ask her to make every sign of age invisible. He wanted a wearable hat, not a false promise that it had never been damaged.

On our next walk, I kept glancing at the patch. Grandfather seemed to forget it. He was watching the river and telling me about a bird near the bank. The hat was back at work, shading his eyes. I realised I had been looking for evidence of the accident while he was using the object again. Both views belonged to its story, but the repair had made it possible to continue that story outside the cupboard.

questions.prompt: How is the hat damaged?
options: It rolls away in the wind and is found with a hole
It is burned in the kitchen
It is cut up for a school model
questions.explanation: Wind rolls hat, retrieved with cloth hole. Other causes/events not described.

questions.prompt: What does the holiday photograph show?
options: The hat had been part of earlier experiences
The hat was bought that morning
Every old object must remain unused
questions.explanation: Older holiday image connects hat/history. Other claims contradict chronology/use.

questions.prompt: What does the grandfather request from the repair?
options: Proof that no damage ever occurred
A wearable hat with a suitable patch
A display case that cannot be opened
questions.explanation: Wants usable repair without hiding age entirely. Replacement/false history/case not requested.

questions.prompt: What changes on the next walk?
options: The grandfather uses the hat while the narrator notices its patch
Both leave the hat locked away
The repairer joins the bird walk
The patch makes the hat unable to shade eyes
questions.explanation: Final paragraph contrasts functional attention with accident evidence. Other options unsupported/opposite.

materials.text:

The school fund now covers admission, so pupils do not bring the six pounds. The café will be closed; everyone needs a packed lunch. Two teachers accompany the twenty pupils. Mina may join us directly and return by coach.

Mina and her parent should meet the school group at the north entrance at09:10. The parent should remain until a teacher takes responsibility. School badges are still required. Bring packed lunches as arranged; no café service is available that day.

materials.title: The bench with one new board
materials.text:
The bench outside our school office had one damaged board. When the caretaker replaced it, the new wood was much lighter in colour than the rest. Several pupils joked that the bench now looked unfinished.

Our class was designing a small history display about the school grounds. I wanted a photograph of the bench, but I waited for the caretaker to paint it so the boards would match. He asked whether the display was about how the grounds looked today or about an imagined moment when every repair was invisible.

I had not meant to hide anything. I simply thought a uniform colour would make the picture tidier. He showed me the work record, which named the board that had been replaced and the date. The repair was part of the bench's present condition, not a mark that the photograph needed to erase.

We took two pictures: one of the whole bench and one of the new board's joint. The display caption explained the recent repair and why only one board had been changed. It did not claim the entire bench was new. Nor did it treat the old wood as worthless merely because one part had failed.

A former pupil recognised the bench in the wider photograph. She remembered waiting there for her brother years earlier. Her memory concerned the object as a place in school life, while our detail photograph showed a particular intervention in it. We displayed her account as a later recollection, with permission.

The caretaker eventually painted the board as planned. We added the new date rather than replace the earlier photograph silently. The display now showed change across a short period. A tidy final image would have been useful, but keeping the sequence allowed visitors to see how an ordinary object continued through repair.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator first delay photographing the bench?
options: To avoid recording any school objects
Because the bench is missing entirely
questions.explanation: Narrator wants uniform colour. Bench exists and project includes it.

questions.prompt: What does the caretaker’s record establish?
options: Which board was replaced and when
That the whole bench is new
That old wood has no value
questions.explanation: Record specific intervention/date, not total replacement or worthlessness.

questions.prompt: Why are two pictures taken?
options: To show both the whole object and the repaired detail
To pretend both were taken years earlier
To remove every sign of change
questions.explanation: Wider/detail images complementary. False old dating/erasure opposite transparent record.

questions.prompt: How is the former pupil’s contribution presented?
options: As words printed on the bench originally
As proof that no repair occurred
As a later recollection with permission
questions.explanation: Memory labelled retrospective, consented; not inscription or denial.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of keeping the earlier photograph?
options: The first repair is falsely called never completed
Visitors can follow the repair sequence
questions.explanation: Before/after dates preserve change. Other outcomes unsupported.
